title: Itô's lemma
description: Brownian motion $X_t = \sigma W_t$ (no potential), all particles at the origin, and the test function $f(x) = e^{x}$. The ordinary chain rule would give $d\,e^{W_t} = e^{W_t}\,dW_t$, a martingale with constant mean 1. Itô's lemma adds the second-order term: $d\,e^{\sigma W_t} = \sigma e^{\sigma W_t}\,dW_t + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}e^{\sigma W_t}\,dt$, so $\mathbb{E}\,e^{\sigma W_t} = e^{\sigma^2 t/2}$ (course notes, §4.1.2.3; compare Remark 3.28). Press play and step with → to stop at a given time.

questions.text: What does the ordinary chain rule predict for $\mathbb{E}\,e^{W_t}$ at every $t$?
Pause at $t = 1$. What is the particle mean of $e^{X^1_t}$?
Restart with σ = 0.5. Value of $\mathbb{E}\,e^{X^1_1}$ now?
Which function of $W_t$ and $t$ is a martingale, so that its mean stays at 1? Use Itô's lemma to check that its $dt$ term vanishes.
The band (95 % confidence interval) gets wider with time although the number of particles stays the same. Why? (Look at the variance of $e^{W_t}$.)
